utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good morning to everyone. May we have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Tom Hannis, Joanna Korner, and Jasmina Bosnjakovic for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Eugene O'Sullivan, Ms. Tatjana Savic appearing for Stanisic Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For Zupljanin Defence, Igor Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zecevic, we were alerted that --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have a matter to raise which I think is the same as Mr. Zecevic's. I'd prefer to raise it, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I don't think that's proper, Ms. Korner, because the matter which we are talking about is the very same, and it is my mistake, and I should be able to explain my mistake before you take the floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, yesterday on transcript 11503, line 14. I proposed to the witness, which was yesterday, during the additional cross-examination, I proposed to him that two villages which were mentioned in that document are Muslim villages. The witness says, "I don't know." Now, I found out only later from the information of my office that, in fact, both these villages are, in fact, purely ethnically Serb villages. So I wanted to apologise to the Trial Chamber and withdraw my question. That is number one issue. The second issue, Your Honours, on page 11457, line 13. We admitted the document 1D324. I called the document by its 65 ter number, which is 65 ter 153. However, after I reviewed this yesterday afternoon I found out that the identical, the similar, document has already been admitted as P867 and has a 65 ter number 2822. So therefore, in order that we don't duplicate -- in order that we don't duplicate the documents, I guess I should -- this document which I offered should be withdrawn and the number deleted from the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, so the order would be to withdraw the number assigned to that last -- to that duplicate admission. Thank you, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry to take a little more time over this, but it's not quite as simple as Mr. Zecevic would like to suggest. As you will recall this arose because of the document that I was showing to Mr. Njegus yesterday about the report from the Trebinje CSB in respect of war crimes committed against Serbs. There was a lot of interruption while we were showing the document, and the document wasn't being put up very clearly. Do you remember the word "genocide" wasn't appearing. I did not understand at the time that Mr. Zecevic's interruptions, because Mr. Krgovic was also interrupting at that stage, were intended that I should show the third page with the -- apart from Visegrad. Now, I had looked at the whole document obviously before I put it to the witness, and, in fact, Your Honour, the suggestion by implication was very clearly that I was deliberately trying to mislead the Court by not showing the witness a part of the document which was contradictory to the proposition that I was exploring with the witness, namely, that all that the Serbs were interested were that it was the reporting of war crimes as against Serbs. And that was absolutely clear. Now, Your Honours, I was -- in the back of my mind that although I hadn't specifically asked about Visegrad because it didn't say it in terms that it was, in fact, a further alleged war crime against Serbs and I so informed Mr. Zecevic before he began his re-cross-examination. At that stage I didn't have the document. And the re-cross-examination is quite important. "However, Ms. Korner said that this report is only about crimes against Serbs, so I would now like you to take a look at page 3, as I've repeatedly asked you to do during her examination," which as I explained to him I simply didn't appreciate this what he wanted me to do. "The SJB of Visegrad has also filed two criminal reports for war crimes, the massacre of ten civilians including two minor children and the killing of one women in the village of Pale." And this is the question and this is what I really -- and I took objection to it at the time. "Do you know that both these villages are Muslim villages?" It is a form of cross-examination that has occurred throughout, effectively the assertion of a fact, and I have already objected to the way these assertions are being made with which the witness is asked to agree. So I assumed that I must have made a mistake and I was wrong when I was of the view that this was also a war crime attack apparently on Serbs that they were reported because it was asserted as such. I assumed that Mr. Zecevic either knew or had strong instructions to that effect because that's the only basis on which such a suggestion could be made in that form. And then, Your Honours, as you know the witness said, "I don't know." Your Honours, after the Court rose yesterday, my attention was drawn to what I had in the back of my mind, and the reason I vaguely remembered it but couldn't lay my hand on it was on the 18th of -- sorry, the -- yes, the 18th of February, I think it was or the 19th, I think it was filed the 19th -- or it's dated the 18th, we made a large -- we -- sorry, we put in a motion to amend our 65 ter list of exhibits, and we divided the documents into categories. And under category D was a document which the categories were those which either recently had come to light or had been overlooked in our researches. And document number -- proposed 65 ter number 03546, municipality of Visegrad, official note from operative Dragan Vukasinovic dated the 2nd of October, and failure to take measures -- the relevance was failure to take measures against perpetrators of crimes committed against non-Serbs. Your Honours denied that motion. The Defence objected to it. And one can assume, therefore, that the Defence went through the documents we were applying to add, and certainly all the documents have been disclosed to them. Your Honours denied that part of the motion and, in fact, it's at the moment still subject to appeal. I would like Your Honours now to have a look -- because effectively my application is that this document now be made an exhibit. Could we put up, please, 10382, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: While the document is being loaded, I would interject that one of the -- when the objection was taken to the question by you, Ms. Korner, I did not appreciate that it was a matter in controversy and I put it in the category that while the objection was technically correct about the effect of the -- the form of the question being counsel giving evidence, I considered it in the category of do you know that London is the capital of the United Kingdom? And that is why I let the matter pass.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, that's the problem. It was a matter of controversy. Mr. Zecevic knew it was a matter of controversy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I now understand that to be the position.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And also I have to say, I assumed that it was being done on instructions at the time, and I understand it may not have been. Your Honours, this is the Official Note, 2nd of October, which refers to the incident which was in that report. "Whilst gathering information on the crime committed against the Serbian people by members of Green Berets, Ustashas in the Visegrad municipality, we obtained certain security information at around 2000 hours on the 1st of August, 1992, in Jelasci village" -- I don't know if I'm pronouncing this right. "Around 10 kilometres from Visegrad the Green Berets committed a crime against the Serbian people the like of which has never been seen in these parts," then describes it. And you will see at the bottom of the English translation "Green Berets shot dead on their door step, driven his wife's Sava" -- and if we go to the next page in English, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Ms. Korner is kindly asked to speak closer to the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry. Can we have the next page in English, please. Could we have the next page in English. Thank you. "They shot dead on their door-step Trivun and his wife Sava and two underaged children." And Your Honours will see that is clearly the incident that was referring to in that report about which I was asking Mr. Njegus about yesterday. So, Your Honours, there are two matters. The first is that, Your Honours, I think the reasoning behind the refusal to allow us to add it to our 65 ter was that we didn't give an actual explanation -- did not indicate the reasons for their late addition beyond asserting they are relevant to the case. My application is now, it is clearly and apparently relevant to what is a major issue in the case between the Prosecution and the Defence, namely, the Prosecution case is that any reference to war crimes against non-Serbs was literally window-dressing and that their only real interest was in investigating crimes committed against Serbs. That is an issue in this case. So therefore, my application -- and particularly in light of what happened, my application is this now that Your Honours effectively add it to our 65 ter list, but admit it as an exhibit. And the second matter is this, and I'm sorry to raise it. Twice in one week the allegation by Defence has been that the Prosecution and myself in particular have attempted to mislead the Court in some way. Your Honour, I take such allegations extremely seriously. They're made in open forum in the public. I wasn't able to obtain an apology from Mr. Pantelic, and I'm not seeking an apology now, but I am seeking that the record is made clear, that at no stage was I ever attempting to mislead the Court on any matter, nor would I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Korner. May I just add on behalf of the Bench that none of us have had any suspicions that you were engaged in such attempts, so we have full trust in you, and we take the remark from the Defence as being nothing more than expressions in the heat of the fight. But can I just return to the first issue that you raised because I'm not sure I fully understand what the situation is, given the fact that Mr. Zecevic has explained that his assumption was wrong, that these two villages were not Muslim, that they were indeed Serb. So my immediate reaction to that would be well then we will disregard that part of the re-cross-examination that came to us yesterday, and if we do so, how does that then impact your assertion today.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You mean my application, Your Honour, to add this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's a further document, and it's quite important. As Your Honours may know because we've heard evidence about Visegrad, Visegrad was the scene of some seriously appalling crimes as against the non-Serb population, for example, the house fire -- well, I don't know that Your Honours have because it was part of the adjudicated facts and it's part of our application to call evidence about it. And that no attempt was made to investigate that -- there's no report about it. There's a report, however, on this. And the whole document, therefore, as I indicated and was suggesting to the witness, is all about the reports of crimes committed against Serbs. And this document, which is the report from the -- Mr. Vukasinovic is part of that document. It's -- it goes along with all the other reports. So -- and, Your Honour, it shows that the whole report -- because it's not clear, you see, that's why I didn't deal with it, because it wasn't actually clearly stated, and in the SJB Visegrad was put in a report about this crime against non-Serbs. This document makes it absolutely clear. It puts the whole report that I read to the witness in context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So if we accede to the application to add it to your 65 ter list, what then?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And to have it made an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Is the -- is there anything that the Defence has to say on the application to add this document to the 65 ter list and thereafter to have it admitted as an exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I clearly admitted my mistake. I withdrew my question. As Judge Harhoff clearly stated, it would be disregarded by the Trial Chamber. And I personally don't have anything against this document, but if we would admit this document as one exception to the rules how we are admitting the document, we are opening the door to more exceptions. So I don't -- I mean, this document was not shown to the witness, the witness didn't know about these villages at all, of course he was not aware of this document. I think at this point, according to our -- the rules which were in place for ten months in this trial, this document has reached the threshold to be MFI'd only, nothing else. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I support submission of my learned friend, Mr. Zecevic, on that issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, this came about, as I said to Judge Harhoff, the document which is based on this doesn't make it clear that this is reporting an attack allegedly on Serbs. Without this document, I can't give evidence. What I've said today about it and really doubt, is not evidence. The document is the evidence that links it to this document. The fact that the witness couldn't recognise it is irrelevant. It's clearly part and parcel of the documentation that's received by the MUP. I suppose I could find another witness who I can ask about this gentleman, but I don't think there's any serious dispute that this is a document that is, on the face of it, what it says it is. And this all came about through the Defence. So exceptional or not, Your Honours, we suggest this is an appropriate time to admitted this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, we note the objection that Mr. Zecevic has raised and accepting the untidiness of this whole exercise and I believe I would have made the observation quite early on in this trial - and I speak personally here - that consistency is -- appearing to be consistent is less important than trying to make the correct decision on each individual occasion. And we think that in the circumstances the relevance of this document is rooted in the point in controversy between the parties as to whether such reports were made in respect of attacks on non-Serb villages, were, as to use Ms. Korner's phrase, window-dressing. In the circumstances we accede to the application both to add it to the 65 ter list and thereafter that it migrate and become an exhibit marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sorry, I will pick up from where I said we accede to the application and notwithstanding what I would have said about it being marked for identification, we allow the document having been -- to be admitted and marked. I was going to say "having been tendered." I'm not sure it was tendered, but the document is somehow before us so we allow it to be admitted and marked. And we remind counsel for the Prosecution that the -- this document is -- forms part of a motion of which the Trial Chamber is now seized to certify for the Appeal Chamber, the previous decision to which counsel has alluded. So the decision that we now make we treat as an application that counsel would have made, as it were, for reconsideration. So that portion of the motion that is still live falls away by virtue of the order that we now make.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. In fact, Your Honour's are quite right. I meant to say that effectively that was how we would have to treat it because there's still an outstanding motion to appeal and, therefore, the appeal is obviously still live but minus this document. Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document will become Exhibit P1424, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If Your Honours forgive me, I will leave the court because Mr. Hannis is going to continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I would like to be heard before my learned friend Ms. Korner is going to leave the court, please. I have to address the Trial Chamber with regard to the issue which was raised by Ms. Korner related to my submission very shortly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Please proceed, but I didn't realise there was something that we were still considering, Mr. Pantelic. I thought we ruled.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Go ahead. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Could you bear with me for a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, Ms. Korner mentioned my name in relation to certain part of submission and allegations that she misleaded the Court, et cetera. First of all, this interpretation was not my intention from my part, to -- to say that she's misleading the Court on that way. My intervention was based purely on the -- in relation to the principles of fairness and professional co-operation between the parties and professional diligence. I'm -- don't have any problem to apologise to Ms. Korner if her impression was that I, to some extent, acted and said something which was not appropriate in accordance with her understanding and knowledge of course. But prior to that, I'm entitled to have her apologise. Namely, and I make my submission on the transcript, it's at page 10869 and 10867 on May 26th. At that day I said that Ms. Korner misquoting me in relation to Traynor's article. And that was the fact, if you are going to see this reference. So she clearly misquoted me and then on the basis of this issue made further submissions, allegedly that I did not object to the admission of all Mr. Traynor's article, et cetera. But okay, that's -- leave all this stuff aside. I would say this is kind of a housekeeping matter that both parties have and then we are discussing one way or another. But we have a more serious problem here, Your Honours. My position is the following: I think and I believe, deeply believe, that certain members of Prosecution, namely, Ms. Korner, is actually performing her duty as a Prosecution attorney expanding the standards of re-direct examination, Your Honour. Please. Yesterday we were witness to that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, I'm sorry, this is enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Counsels are expected to behave professionally and diligently in court. These accusations back and forth of who is trying to mislead or twist the reality is something that you have to fight outside the courtroom. And we all accept that sometimes in the heat of the fight parties may inadvertently come to express views that perhaps they should not have done; and if they do so, the easiest and the simplest thing between human beings is to reach out your hand and to give an apology. And other than that, I think there is nothing more to it. I suggest that we stop this now and bring the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I fully appreciate what you said, but for the record, I must put on the record because this is a serious issue, We think that principles of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, the issue is closed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Our next witness is Dragan Kezunovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kezunovic, could you please read once again the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may be seated. Can you please for the record state your name and your date of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Dragan Kezunovic. I was born on the 20th November, 1946.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. What was your profession in 1992, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was employed with the republic secretariat for internal affairs in Sarajevo as assistant chief of administration for communications.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. And what is your occupation today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm retired.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: What is your ethnicity, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Serb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Is this the first time you are testifying before this Tribunal or before a Tribunal in your country on these matters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it's the first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. You have been called as a witness for the Prosecution. That means that the Prosecution will start asking you questions. Prosecution asked for four hours to do so. After that, the Defence, on that side, will cross-examine and ask questions also; after which, the Prosecution can re-examine, re-direct, ask you some more questions. And after all that, it's -- eventually the Bench, the Judges, could ask you questions. Is that clear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: We sit in sessions of 90 minutes, 20-minutes' pause; 90 minutes, 20-minutes' pause; and a last 90 minutes. So three sessions of 90 minutes each time with a pause of 20 minutes for technical reasons. If for any reason you feel uncomfortable and need an extra break or a pause, just let us know. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Kezunovic. I see that you are currently retired. Could you tell us when you retired from the MUP?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I received the decision on the 15th February, 2002.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And how long had you worked in the MUP at the time you retired?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: You mean in total, before the war and during the war?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, in both the RS MUP and the Bosnian MUP.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: From the 1st of March, 1978.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what positions did you hold, what jobs did you do in the MUP when you worked for them, if you can briefly tell us?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The internal organisation of the MUP changed several times during my tenure, but generally speaking, until the war, I was always deputy chief, whether he was chief of sector or chief of department, or chief of administration. And when he, the chief, retired, I became chief of communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When did that first happen, that you became chief?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: With the beginning of the conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina, that means early April when I was invited to the MUP of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, as it was called then by definition. The post of chief of communications was offered to me, and I accepted.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Before that, if I can ask you, in the summer, July of 1991, what position did you hold and where were you working?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I was chief of section within the administration for communications, and ex officio I was also chief of -- deputy chief of administration. However, since the post of chief was vacant, I was acting chief. I believe it was in June/July, that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And physically, geographical speaking, where were you working?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: At the base of the republic secretariat for internal affairs in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'd like to show you now an exhibit that's already in evidence in this case. This is P897. And I don't think this is one that you've seen before, but I believe you'll be able to offer some comment on it. And I would tell you to start with, this is an intercepted telephone conversation between Radovan Karadzic and Vitomir Zepinic. Did you know Mr. Zepinic in 1991?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And with the usher's help, I could hand the witness a hard copy. It might be easier for him to follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The part I want to start with, Mr. Kezunovic, is on the second page of the document you have, and Mr. Karadzic is talking to Mr. Zepinic about positions in the MUP held by Serbian personnel. Because you'll recall at this time after the nationalist parties had come into power, there were certain agreements about who would hold various positions in the various organs in the government. Is that correct so far?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It is correct that parties had an internal agreement between them about the distribution of all senior posts in the secretariat for internal affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in English, for Your Honours, if you're following along, at the very bottom of the page Mr. Karadzic says: "To take a position whether it's good or not. Now I see, I have to sign here," going on to page 3, "I have to sign here, something that Simovic sent to me for some Kezunovic, whom I don't know, but to be transferred from MUP to the defence ministry where Doka is." And Mr. Zepinic says: "Dragan Kezunovic?"

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC SAYS
utterances.text: "Dragan Kezunovic." And if you'll follow on to the bottom of your second page a little further on Mr. Karadzic says: "At communications, we have another man for communications at the ministry to tie up with Doka, but we mustn't risk losing one place at the SUP ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEPINIC SAYS
utterances.text: "The post is important to me. That's an engineering post and it's very important for the man to be a professional here and the communications system at the ministry." Karadzic asks if Zepinic knows you. And then going on to page 3 for you he says: Zepinic says he was here this morning. He asks what you're like. Zepinic tells him you're the son of Slobodan. And at the bottom of page 4 in English and still on your page 3 Zepinic asks: "Well, who should I get instead of Kezunovic?" And Karadzic says: "Well, no, Kezunovic should stay if that's what's of interest to us." In July of 1991, were you aware of any discussions or a plan to shift you from the MUP to the Defence ministry? Did you know that was being discussed?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. Nobody ever told me, nobody ever asked me anything about going to the Ministry of Defence, but there are other facts from this conversation that I am aware of. I will either explain or you will ask me about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, first let me ask you. So I take it you did not move, you did not move from the Ministry of the Interior or the secretariat of interior; you remained in that position until the war broke out, and you eventually went and worked for the RS MUP. Correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you said you -- there were other facts that you're aware of. Could you briefly tell us what those are?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I can. It all has to do with this text you've just read. I said I was head of a section and the chief of that section would always be deputy chief of the administration, since the post of chief was vacant and I was told that this post was subject to internal agreement and was envisaged to go to the SDA and the person to be appointed to that post should be a member of the SDA, a Muslim. But since the SDA didn't propose anyone for a long time, I was invited by the head of personnel, Mr. Selimovic, he was also a member of the SDA, who told me something like this. You and I know each other well. You're an engineer, a trained engineer. You have been in this post a long time. Stay in that job. Mind only your job and pay no heed to anything else. And that's what I did. However, the problems started when the chief was finally appointed. It was an engineer, who had worked in telecom previously, and the first thing that happened was that he invited me to his office to tell me that within an hour I should advise him of my departure from the Ministry of Interior and which job I found next. Nobody mentioned the Ministry of Defence or anything else at that point. I had an argument with the man. I told him it was not something that he was supposed to or could decide according to the rules and regulations and that I would continue in my job whether he liked it or not. And that's what happened. I remained in my job, but my coming to work was practically just a formality from that time on. Nobody gave me anything to do, and I was not involved in the work in any practical terms. I was just physically present at work, spoke to the other employees about the job and some current problems. And one day I ran into Mr. Zepinic and complained to him about all that. He was then deputy minister. And this conversation between Zepinic and Karadzic was perhaps partly a result of my complaint to Mr. Zepinic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What was the name of the chief who told you to leave?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Akif Sabic. I forgot to say a moment ago that at that time I did not belong to any political party. I was not affiliated at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That was my next question. Did you ever belong to a political party after 1991?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. You mentioned having a conversation with Mr. Zepinic, telling him about this problem. Was he able to do anything for you that you're aware of in terms of fixing the problem?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, he was probably able to help only by preventing them from forcing me to resign and remain jobless. That's actually what I was asking him to do. I asked him also to find me any post, any engineering post, in that service. It didn't have to be a senior post. And he was probably able to do that and he might have done it actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I'm sorry, I forgot to ask you earlier. What kind of training did you have to hold the jobs that you eventually held? What was your educational background?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I can. I graduated from the school of electrical engineering of the University of Sarajevo, and in the last year of my studies I received a scholarship from telecom. It was at that time a large conglomerate in PTT services, and I started working after graduation for telecom. However, after a while I transferred to the republic secretariat of internal affairs at their own request. They invited me for an interview and offered me the post of engineer in charge of development and modernisation of the internal communications system. While I was working still in telecom, I was in charge of maintenance of hardware in transit switchboards, of which there were 23 or 24 in the territory of the former Yugoslavia. At that time it was almost state-of-the-art technology. So I was assigned to that job and I worked on the maintenance of hardware in the central management unit, but later on when I transferred to the republic secretariat I completed almost every year an advanced training course in a particular specialty to keep up with the advancement of technology in the world. We had to attend courses and to keep up, especially courses concerning the protection of data.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, I think you said earlier that you were invited to come work for the newly created Serbian MUP, which later became the Republika Srpska MUP. When approximately did that happen, do you remember the date that you were first contacted about doing that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, that was -- but before that I need to explain something else and I will be brief of course. My father hails from Sokolac, the municipality of Sokolac, which is 40 kilometres from Sarajevo. We had a family house there. This house was set to fire in December of 1990 by someone. At the time of course it was not possible to do anything about fixing it, and as of that moment I travelled every day to Sokolac so that I'd just be present there and to take care of the remains of that house. The first floor and part of the roof burned down, and then the water and the cold destroyed the bottom part of the building as well. So until the time of the breakout of the war, I would go every day and spend the night in this house in Sokolac and then take the bus to Sarajevo in the morning. I don't know the exact dates, but it was in late March when barricades started appearing in Sarajevo. There were also various protest gatherings of -- I can't even remember who anymore. And the barricades were set up at the entry points to the town. It was in the first weekend in April and then the days immediately following, Monday, Tuesday, that the bus could not pass through the barricades. It had to stop before them, but these barricades were set up by both sides along the road from Sokolac and Pale. The Serbs had their check-point and at the exit point from the town near the town hall, the Muslims, the Green Berets, had theirs. I'd noticed one even earlier because that's usually where I would wait for the bus for Sokolac and also this was the place where I would step off my bus on my way in. So it was for two days in a row that I could not come to my place of employment. My colleagues from down there were calling me, and I explained why I couldn't come to work. Also, please understand, I was not surprised by the situation and the conditions that morning, but the events were unfolding in such a way that it was only a matter of days when this would happen. And now I'm answering to your question. I apologise. So it was in the period between the 5th and the 10th of April when I received a call from communications officer who was also from Sokolac and who was most probably at Pale at the time, telling me that Mr. Stanisic would like to speak to me; and then I was offered the position. But since everything was clear by then and one could tell where things were going to go, I accepted the job. That's in brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. What was the name of the person who called you and told you that Mr. Stanisic was wanting to speak to you about working at the newly formed Serb MUP?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It was a communications officer who worked as an operator, Zoran Borovcanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did you talk with Mr. Stanisic on the phone, or did you go see him in person? How did that take place?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I went to Pale, and I followed the instructions Zoran gave me, and that's where I met with Mr. Stanisic and where everything was arranged.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Had you known Mr. Stanisic before?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And that's Mico Stanisic we're talking about?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What did he tell you when you had that conversation?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, to the effect of: You see how things are developing. Please bear in mind that I used to work for the police. I knew about what was going on in general terms in the wider area. This was just - let me put it like this - an official confirmation that things seemed to be going in a certain way. I realised I had not much choice. I accepted the post, especially because this was a kind of post that involved my expertise that I was good at. So I thought there shouldn't be any problems there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And to be precise, what post was it that he offered you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Chief of administration for communications or chief of communications, as we would internally call it. Now, at the time whether it had -- because at the time we didn't have an official document explaining internal systemisation, and the terminology used was such to be analogous to the pre-war systemisation. I was offered a post of deputy minister or chief of that administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did he give you any particular task upon your acceptance of the position as chief of communications?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Nothing special. He told me there's no need for me to explain things to you. You know well enough what is necessary. I only asked where is the starting location, so to speak, what is our starting point? What needs to be linked up into the system. And I was told it would be Pale and then we'll see how things developed on the ground. And according to that, we'll be organising our communications system.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And after that, what did you do then? Did you stay in Pale and try to get things right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, to tell you the truth, the question was put, it was put in a brief form and clear, but the answer is more complex -- yet, I will try and answer you in a brief manner. When you come to a location where there's nothing, you don't have the premises, you don't have the devices, you don't have the personnel, you don't have documentations according to which you should be working, it is clear from all that that the initial starting point, initial location, was zero. Nothing could have been done overnight, of course, or in a brief period of time. Things had to be done in proper order to see who was available, who's available of people with expertise, communication expertise, who used to work in former republican SUP. And I'm not talking only about the headquarters, but in broader terms, the town SUP or the city of Sarajevo SUP, the municipal secretariats. And then to see what kind of equipment we can find. So we spent a few days in the initial stage to have -- having consultations with people from our profession. It was very difficult to establish communication because at the time initially the communications were not functioning because they were switched off. Later on some of the relays were later on destroyed. So the infrastructure was not present. In the first few days I used to go back to Sokolac to spend the night there. On occasions, of course, I had to sleep in the building where we met, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: After you accepted the job, then did you stay in Pale; and if so, for how long?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I stayed for several days. I cannot tell you precisely how many, but it was for a shorter period of time. And then, after receiving an order by the minister, I went to the school -- to a school in Sarajevo, to the school of internal affairs. And me and several associates went there to the premises of that school to check whether the headquarters of the ministry could be located there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the school you're talking about, that's the one that was located at Vrace, if I'm pronouncing that correctly?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The school -- or rather, this was a centre for education of internal affairs staff, including as well a high school for internal affairs four years, and upon graduating from that, one would become a police officer. And it was called centre for education of police staff. It was called like that because all the courses were being organised there which the --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt. My question, though, was just: Is that the location that's sometimes referred to as Vrace?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And -- thank you. And you say you went there after receiving an order by the minister. Was that a written order or just a verbal order, to go to Vrace?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It was a verbal order. I even wasn't told that by him. The colleagues who went along, one of them or several of them told me who should be in that group, initial group, and that was all.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Next I'd like to show you Exhibit P541. I have a hard copy of this one for you as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Could we have a tab, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry. It's tab 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you will have seen this one, Mr. Kezunovic, during proofing I think. It's the record of a meeting of a board of directors at the police academy on the 14th of April, 1992. And you'll see you're listed as one of those attending the meeting. Do you recall having been at such a meeting?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I want to ask you about on your first page, I think it's the second paragraph. It says, "There's a gap between Pale and the Serbian MUP. The minister and the under-secretary and all the others are in Pale." Was that a source of some difficulties in getting things started in the first week or two after the split of the former MUP?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, based on what I see in the document, my understanding of this gap is bad communications or poor communications, which then makes it difficult to communicate between Vrace and other locations, primarily Pale, the minister and his immediate associates. I assume that the gap mentioned here is that gap. And let me just clarify one more thing. Before the war, in entire Yugoslavia and in Bosnia and Herzegovina as well, the police had its own system of communications and let me tell you what it implied. But also, all other major state systems, like power system -- electrical power system, TV, they all had internal systems. It wasn't only the police, but one of the specific elements of the police system was that it had capacity of the kind where the communication between different cities and towns linking up police elements and units was done in accordance to hierarchy. So when we're talking about the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, it was like that. And when we're talking about the city of Sarajevo and some of the other cities in the republic, the police had teleprinter communication because at the time we didn't have computers, we used teleprinters. And we had our own cable connections that linked up all police buildings and state facilities for the purpose of security and protection of state organs and other facilities that the police was in charge of security-wise. So the school at Vrace was also linked-up with two cables, the public cable and the police cable. But that went through the Telekom building, which was after several days -- the communication was switched off because the Telekom building was in Sarajevo. We could see it from Vrace, the building by the communication was switched off. We managed to find some people who lived in the neighbourhood and we asked them to lend us two phone numbers so that we would have some sort of communication. But we couldn't use these two numbers for anything confidential, for instance, we could not exchange written messages -- and I'm talking about the first few days here. And yes, that's why they're speaking about the gap in communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And were you able to use those two phone numbers you borrowed from some people living in the area to communicate with Pale during those first few days, although you could only do it for open conversations?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I have to add one more thing. These two numbers, we had our police officers who gave us the numbers. It was the police officers or their relatives. It wasn't us or the service who did that. It was done independently of me. Once the cables in the Telekom building were cut off. Now, I can't remember whether these people were relatives of one of our police officers or neighbours, but it was along those lines that we got hold of the two telephone numbers. And then I think later on even these two numbers were switched off because they were all part of the same switchboard.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If I may, one more question before we break.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You see -- I think it may be on page 2 of your document, there's a section where you're listed as speaking, and you talk about you don't have enough people and there are big communication problems in the field. And the last thing you're noted as saying, it says: "According to the agreement with the Serbian S SUP and the Serbian MUP, we should request the equipment they can give us." Serbian S SUP, does that mean the federal SUP in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you recall now what the agreement was under which you might request equipment from them?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It was not any special agreement. A group of us that were in the supervisor position there at Vrace, we sat together. The people mentioned in the document, including myself, we sat there and tried to discuss the options of overcoming our problems. And when my turn came -- well, I would have said it anyhow. It was logical of course. You must understand, at the time, you must understand me and my position. For me, Yugoslavia was my state, not Bosnia and Herzegovina. Bosnia and Herzegovina was part of the state of Yugoslavia. And as long as the federal SUP existed, which was the top of the pyramid for all the republics, I had my expectations from them and that was what my comment was about. I don't know who else one could have asked at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It's time for our first recess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. We resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Kezunovic, I have wanted to make one request. I know it's your first time testifying, and I appreciate your sincere desire to give us as much information as possible, but I'd like to ask you to try and keep your answers as short as possible depending on the question. But also, if you feel you need to add something to clarify, please let us know and I'll be happy to let you do that. The only reason I say this is because I'm under a time-limit and I have a lot of things I want to try and cover with you. And having said that and looking at the transcript, I realise I may not have gotten a complete answer to one of my recent questions. Regarding the time you were at Vrace, You mentioned the phone lines being cut or turned off, and you - meaning I guess individual police officers through family members in the area - were able to get two telephone numbers that you were able to use. And my question was: Were you able to use those two telephone numbers to communicate by phone from Vrace to Pale during those early days?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Generally, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And the document that we were looking at of the meeting of the 14th --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Could I just ask --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: -- you also mentioned that the lines were cut off at some point. When was that, do you recall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember the exact date, but it was several days after we arrived at Vrace. Simply when the folks in town realised that someone is in that installation, that it's occupied, that it's -- something is going on there, they intercepted the conversations because the cable which connected the Vrace building with the Ministry of the Interior passed through the building of Telekom, and Telekom was a very visible building in town. It was approximately 1 kilometre away as the crow flies. You simply pull out the fuses and stop the connection, or you can do it through software at the switchboard. You can disconnect certain numbers. But in this particular case, the cable was disconnected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: It's just because the issue of communication is an important issue in this trial. So are you able to approximately remember how long time these two phone lines were available to you? That's all we need to know. Just approximately.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know even this. There was a short period when the cables were disconnected. We had no telephone communication at all for a couple of days. I can't tell you the exact number of days, but for a couple of days we had no telephone communication at all. We only had one amateur short-wave radio station, radio transceiver for ham radio operators, but that's not something that we professionally would use because everybody can listen to these air waves and practically anyone can intercept. So that sort of communication, even if it existed, was completely unsuitable for confidential exchanges. I don't know what was going on at the time that was very important or confidential. That's another matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Back to you, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: During that time when you had no phones for a couple of days, did you have any other means to communicate with Pale besides this amateur short-wave radio station, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Maybe it was possible, but that too would have been completely insecure and unreliable to use the radios, portable radios that police officers normally carry. Because the local repeater located at Pale covered the area of Pale, and the repeater that could cover the broader area of Sarajevo was located at Mount Trebevic. But there anyone could listen to those communications. When I say "anyone," meaning the police force on either side, anyone. Anyone with the -- with an amateur radio would have the scanning option, scan various frequencies, and when you catch on a signal you stop. That was completely unreliable. It was better to get into a car, spend half an hour or an hour driving to Pale, and then have a conversation face-to-face.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That was my next question. Did you communicate by using couriers or driving to Pale and speaking directly with someone during that time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: If you mean me personally, I did not organise any courier service. Whether people could send messengers to carry messages, they could. When I was faced with a need to deal with other problems, not only the problem of communication between Vrace and Pale, of course I was able to go there myself and from there I had a better orientation of what was going on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours. I note that parts of the answers -- the previous answer, the one before that, and this one were not recorded. I think either the witness should be cautioned to speak slowly so that everything he says would be recorded. Because I think it's important. Because there was a sentence after the sentence on 32, 10/11, when witness said whether people could send messages, to carry messages, they could. And then he explained on that but it wasn't recorded. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Kezunovic, you heard that. Do you recall what you said after the part of your answer where you said: "Whether people could send messengers to carry messages, they could." Mr. Zecevic said then what you said next was not recorded in the transcript. Do you remember what else you said because I don't know?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I'm sorry, now I am confused because the gentleman mentioned page 31. I don't know in which document. I have three pages in front of me --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, that was a reference to the page number on the electronic transcript. It's on the computer screen that he was referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I don't know what else I can do, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis. We will have to ask for a verification or maybe in the cross-examination I can clarify that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Kezunovic, I want to show you another document that arises out of the reference here to maybe getting equipment from the Serbian MUP or the federal SUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we show the witness 65 ter number 1943. This is at tab 32.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This is just a short document, so I'll see if we can work with it on the screen. And, Mr. Kezunovic, do you recognise what that is? It's dated the 8th of May, 1992, and mentions the federal secretariat of the interior for the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. It appears to be a list of various kinds of communications equipment.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Could you move the list for me to see all of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And then there's a second page we can show you when you're ready.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: This is probably a set for a short-wave transceiver, short-wave radio. This is the breakdown of this set. It's a short-wave radio station with accessories and installations, power feed, Teletype, various connection cables, the micro telephone combination --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Sorry, let me stop you there. Right above the list of items you'll see a sentence that in my English translation reads: "Following the order of the federal secretariat, we are delivering to you equipment and devices necessary for establishment of the radio-teletypewriter centre for the needs of the SR BH MUP."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we go to the second page of this document in both English and B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's a continuation of the list of the component parts of the set.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And at the bottom of the page we see a couple of signatures. Do you recognise any of those?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I recognise my signature, my own signature; and the other one I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you receive this equipment from someone on or about the date of 8 May 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Do you mean whether I personally received it or whether the MUP received it, someone on behalf of my service?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Most probably, most probably one of my employees received the set, inspected its completeness, and gave me a list to sign because I was the head of that administration. That's -- that was the procedure then.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The signature on the left-hand side of the page is under typewriting that is translated as for SSUP, for the federal secretariat of the interior, equipment handed over. Did you meet that person? Did that person come in and present a document to you, or was it somebody from your own service who gave you the document already signed by somebody from the federal SUP, do you remember?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Right. That's how it was. That's how it worked. I received it from my service. I don't know exactly who gave it to me now, but it was at Pale that I signed it. That's where I was given it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I understand your earlier answer to be that you didn't personally receive all these items on the list, but I assume that if indeed this equipment had not been delivered at some point in time you would have found out that you didn't receive the equipment; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd like to tender this document, 65 ter 1943.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: A list of radio equipment that was -- so it was like a shopping list. So what --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What is important, Your Honour, that this is received from the federal SUP. Part of our case is there's a joint criminal enterprise working with Mr. Milosevic and other individuals in Serbia. It's important to show the co-operation between the former Federal Republic of Serbia [sic] and the newly created Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1425, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours, just one comment. This document refers to the equipment received from the federal secretariat of security, so it doesn't have anything to do -- it is recorded as -- Mr. Hannis has Federal Republic of Serbia. It's the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, SFRY. And it says SSUP, which means the federal MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I -- I'm sorry, I guess if that's what I said, I misspoke. I read earlier the title of the document which says SFR Yugoslavia at the top of the page. I certainly didn't intend to mislead you. It's the federal SUP is my understanding. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, I wanted to ask you about the types of communications equipment you had for use in the Republika Srpska MUP in 1992. You've mentioned telephones. Did you also have Teletype machines and teleprinters?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: May I ask one -- or rather, two things. First of all, can I give my comment first about this equipment that was delivered, this device, this set that was provided on the previous list?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If you can do it briefly, sure.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Here is why. I have told you and I can't remember in response to which question, for me at this moment, chronologically speaking, the federal secretariat for internal affairs was hierarchically directly superior to the secretariat I was working for. And everything that was going on in Bosnia and Herzegovina, the break-up, the collapse of the system, was just beginning. It was the month of April. Until that moment, perhaps due to my upbringing -- but in any case for me it was a completely legal institution that had appropriate equipment envisaged by the war plan --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm sorry. I didn't want to get into a discussion with you about the legality. This is an issue better left for the Judges. But if there's something else you want to say about it, please do. But again, keep it short if you can.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I have nothing else. The whole point was that for me in my eyes it was completely legal.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I wanted to ask you about the types of means of communication that you had in the Republika Srpska MUP in 1992 for communicating between MUP headquarters, the five CSBs, and the SJBs. Can you tell the Judges what those were, just kind of list the equipment available.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: If you mean the MUP headquarters on the Serbian side, you mean, Serbian MUP, in our headquarters we had very little equipment. We had a certain number of telephone plug-ins from the local switchboard of Pale. We had one short-wave radio, and we had several ultra short-wave radios. Those are the networks used by police officers on the beat. We had one or two teleprinters that could work via telephone lines, and there were devices onto which you would plug-in a teleprinter on one side and a telephone connection on the other side, and that's how you would get a telegraph -- teleprinter connection between two teleprinters or Teletypes. But that was the barest minimum because only one operator could work at a time, and if you need to communicate with five points you have to deal with them one by one, and I suppose it's all clear. If you have a short dispatch, to note down, it can be done; but if it's something longer, then it's very difficult. But that only worked until the moment Telekom found a way to provide alternative communication lines on the Serbian side. It's only when the postal system was inter-connected internally, then we got from them two or -- one or two channels to connect our devices onto. It's like a leopard skin, and you have to connect the spots into one whole. Now, for the purposes of documents and coded documents, work-plans, and all the background material that all the participants need to have, it was impossible to achieve at the beginning. Only when you get into direct contact with them, you hand them physically all these documents, the encryption tables, et cetera, on the condition, of course, that they have the right personnel for it. In some places it went quicker, in others slower.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You also had fax machines?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: We did, but under the regulations on data protection and in my view the fax was a completely insecure, unprotected device and you couldn't transmit anything confidential through it. Let me just say one more thing. All that I'm saying about rules and regulations, I mean regulations applying to communication centres, operators, professionals, who are encryptors, part of the communication system, whether anyone outside communications centres was violating these rules is something I wouldn't know. Whenever I got reports about something like that, I reacted, but there are things I may not have known about.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But you did receive reports during 1992 that sometimes MUP employees were, for example, using the fax to send communications that should have gone by a more secure means; is that right ?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I didn't understand the question. Did I see? Is that the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, the last part of your previous answer was, "whenever I got reports about something like that, I reacted ..." and you were referring to when anyone outside communication centres was violating these rules about encrypted communications. And I took that to mean that you did hear that that happened some time. And I thought we've seen some -- during proofing some examples of faxes that were sent, which in your view probably should have been sent by a more secure means. Correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I think we saw it in one of the meetings you attended, that that was something you complained about to your boss, that people weren't following the regulations about how to use communications equipment to ensure the best protection of data?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: That's correct. That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And as you said before, one other means that you could use to send information or communications would be couriers, human beings?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: That's right, but that was not envisaged within my service, within communications. In theory, somebody could give an assignment to the courier, but then you would need drivers, vehicles, fuel, a number of other things that I, in my administration, in my line of work, did not dispose of. I did not even have enough vehicles for my own requirements, let alone organising a service like that. You would need the staff, you would need -- it's not as simple as that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand. Let me go next to another topic. Just in general terms about the level and functioning of communication in the RS MUP in 1992, you're aware of an annual report that was prepared about the working of the MUP for that time-period between April and the end of December 1992. I'd like to have you look at Exhibit P625, and because this is a lengthy document I'll hand you a hard copy with help from the usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, tab number, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. This is tab number 88.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you've seen this report before, Mr. Kezunovic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if we could look first at page -- it's page 23 of the English. And for you, Mr. Kezunovic, I think it's the page number 28 in the bottom right-hand side.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In e-court the B/C/S is page number 32. And it's the second paragraph up from the bottom for you, Mr. Kezunovic. It talks about: "On average, 15 dispatches a day were sent to the centres and other organs from the MUP headquarters (a total of 4170 in all lines of work) and on average 16 dispatches a day were received (a total of 4400)." I have a question for you about the definition of dispatch in your communications centre, and let me explain a little bit. For me in English "dispatch" I think has a more generic meaning, and it can mean sort of any official document or maybe a military document or a news report. But I gather from what I've read and heard from other witnesses that dispatch has a more narrow meaning. Could you tell the Judges what your understanding of a dispatch is in terms of the RS MUP communications work.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: A dispatch in principle is something that has to be urgently sent. It's an order, information, some requested data that is being exchanged among the operational services, and it should be urgently sent to the other side or to a number of sides. And the word comes from the French word "depeche" to hurry, meaning that some information has to be conveyed to somebody else as urgently as possible, who then in turn needs to do something on the basis of the contents of that dispatch. In principle, it should be a brief document because the -- and there are dispatches that are conveyed openly in their original state and dispatches that are conveyed in a coded manner. There was a rule-book that defined what a dispatch should contain, which elements it should contain, formally speaking, heading, what should be contained in the heading, the addressees, the content of the dispatch, the signature. The format was precisely defined, who is the drafter, who is to be the recipient of the dispatch. In order to make everything even more precise, records were kept of all the dispatches incoming and outgoing in all the communications centres, all dispatches that were received at the window, as we call it, at the door of the communications centre, would be recorded in the books of open and coded dispatches. There are also signed degrees of urgency, and it is known within which period of time they would have to be delivered. This is dated in the heading. Records are kept of those sent out and those received, and such books are being held -- maintained also at all the centres where the dispatches originate, and records are kept at the end where they are received. This is maintained, these records, both in the units that are sending out and receiving the dispatches as well as at the communications centres.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In terms of this annual report, the section -- part of the section that we're looking at now and beginning on page 25 of the English and 32 in your copy, there's a section about the task and duties of communications and cryptographic data protection. Did you, Mr. Kezunovic, as chief of that administration have input into this annual report; and if so, how was that done?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Of course. I had my own report, the report from my administration which was done on the basis of input or reports drafted by the centres. The centres did their reports on the basis of reports of the public security stations. The centres would compile all the statistical data, they would process all the aspects of certain issues, as they saw it out in their own area of activities, the conditions of operation, the technology of all the systems. They would process -- perhaps if they had a problem with a shortage of something, if they had personnel problems, any problems would be analytically processed and sent to the centre. The centres would compile all the data and send it to the MUP seat. And then on the basis of their reports and the reports done by the unit at the SUP seat would make an overall report that would encompass the work of all the organs in the communications sector. We would carry out the analysis on the basis of methodology in practice, and then this would be some sort of summary taking out all the relevant parts from different reports from the point of view of an analysis. It would be the item that dealt with the work of the communications section, some problems would be dealt with, and also the statistical data would be provided about the number of dispatches sent out and received. This was always done this way. Except before the war data would be given about the quantity of information because the number of dispatches, for example, one dispatch would -- could be equal to ten smaller ones. But when you sum up the information, then you would be able to present that more specifically as far as the quantity of information was concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And, as I understand it then, the various administrations within the MUP at headquarters, for example, 01, uniformed police; 02, crime prevention; I think communications, you were 04, each of those administrations submitted their own report based on what they received from the centres, which was based on what the centres received from the SJBs. Am I right so far?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, you are. That's how it should be.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Who then took all that -- all those reports from the administration heads like yourself and created this report? Who in the MUP did that, either a person by name or a section by name?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The administration for analysis and data or information would do that. I would give my report to the -- to my secretary and tell her, "Take it and hand it over to the secretary for the administration for analysis," probably the others did the same thing. They would send somebody to deliver the report because it was all in the same building. The analysis chief would either personally or would send someone to ask if this was really a summary of all the most important information because this is a shorter report than my original report was. And then -- so we would agree on all of these matters before the summary on a particular topic would be included in the final report.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I think that partly answered my next question. You had an opportunity to review what the analytical folks had put into the complete report in terms of what it said about your section; is that right? You had a chance to object if you felt they left out something important or wrote something incorrect, is that right, you had an opportunity? And having looked at the report and what it says about your section, is it accurate?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Is the data that is here in the report accurate?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, yes, it is. Yes, although I could perhaps express certain things differently, stylistically in order to make it more understandable for those who were not so involved in the technical aspects. Maybe something there could be a little different, more adequately expressed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I understand that. Let me ask you a question about -- it's English page 27 in e-court, and your hard copy, Mr. Kezunovic, I think it's page -- at the bottom of page 33. And in e-court the B/C/S is page 37. This is an entry in the section about communications and cryptographic data protection. And there's a breakdown here between open and coded dispatches. You see that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think we have to go to the very bottom of the -- or, I'm sorry, the very top of the English page. Yeah. We have it here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And then going on to the next page in e-court, in the B/C/S, and for you I think over to the top of the next page, Mr. Kezunovic, there's a reference to how many short-wave radio connections were established from the communications centre base during that time-period. You see that? And the communications centre base, was that a base that was at MUP headquarters? Where was that physically located?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Each organ from the republican SUP via the security centres in the former Bosnia and Herzegovina down to the municipal secretariat, 109 municipalities, ten centres, and some other units, had short -- a short-wave radio station. This network was built before the war, equipment was procured, and it was operational, but it worked exclusively as a reserve system. That was the intention. When none of the other means of communication were working, then the short-wave network would be initiated. This was done before the war, and it functioned more easily because machine coding was used, teleprinters, Teletypes, and some other devices which did not require the code technicians to do all of that by hand. And it operated in the fastest possible way that the technology at the time allowed. This network that is being referred to in this report did keep the same number of connections, but only in setting up the communications, to set up the communications and to gauge their quality because we treated it also as a spare, reserve, system. When nothing else was working, this was our backup. And this backup, since it was a backup and was not used in its regular -- in the regular operations in order to be able to check its conditions, we would use it from time to time according to a plan so that the participants in the network could check the communications, check the quality, and then the communication would be broken. There was no information actually confirmed -- conveyed over the network. I would issue an internal order for them to, let's say, put together two simple sentences and to convey that text on the network in order to check whether the system was working, to see if there were no errors anywhere in the system.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: My question is specifically that location that's referred to there, communications centre base. Can you tell me physically, geographically, where that was located. If somebody said Mr. Kezunovic is in the communications centre base, where would I go to find you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question. My headphones fell off.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
