utterances.text: I saw that. I'm trying to find out where this communications centre base that's referred to in the annual report, where was that physically located, geographically speaking? If I were trying to find someone who was in the communications centre base, what building would I go to?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but I don't see where it says "base." In this part of the text where we're talking about the short-wave radio communications, is that there?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. In my English translation at least it says "9.585 short-wave radio connections were established from the communications centre base ..." So that sounds like a place, a physical location; and if so, can you tell me where it was?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: In this text there is no sentence like that, but regardless of that there was no base as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Seat of the communications centre, yes, yes, that is a different sense. From the seat, from the communications centre, from the communications centre. That was in the same building as the MUP. Each public security centre and each public security station, there are premises where the communications centre is placed. This is the communications centre. It's just a -- perhaps a terminology issue, a clumsy use of a particular word. There is no base as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: This is just a regular communications centre where all the communications equipment and personnel is located. So this would be in the centre, security -- public security centre or the public security station depending on the facility.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I guess my question is: The communications centre from which 9.585 short-wave radio connections were established, was that in MUP headquarters communications centre?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think that this is an error, from the seat of the communications centres in the whole of the network, because if the MUP were to carry out 9.585 connections, it would need to do only that, nothing else. I think this means all the communications all over. They're planned in a hierarchical structure.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. In addition to MUP's communication network, did some of the other large organs or bodies have their own separate communications networks? For example, the army, the VRS, did they have a separate communications network?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, yes. But their communication directly - well, how can I put it? Ours was also part of the operative services but in a slightly different way. As for the military system, for example, before combat began there was radio silence. Nobody's allowed to use the radio communications before combat starts. Only once combat action was initiated were they able to move -- to use the radio communications, but they also have fixed communications systems, they also have mobile systems which are used by the units that are actually in the field, but I'm not familiar with that type of organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I think you explained to me that between the police you had a primary system that you relied on and a backup system or a reserve system. Can you explain to us what those were for the police?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It's the same system but there are two versions of it. I will explain it in the easiest way if I just talk about telephone communications. Telephone communications comprise - and now I'm speaking in the most simple language, to persons who are not experts in this - there are telephone exchanges of different hierarchical level that have to be linked, they have to be inter-linked. So we have these two systems that you referred to. You actually referred to the manner in which these exchanges are linked together. They are either linked by cable relay systems or by radio relay systems. For us in the MUP what was interesting was to have as many as possible of these connections via cable because that's the securest way. It's -- goes under the surface. They're dug-in and it's not possible to have leaks, unwanted leaks. And because of that we would want as much as possible of the information to go through the cables and avoid having them go over the radio relay system. We consider the radio relay system as a backup system.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And for the military, which was their primary and which was their backup?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I know this in principle the army had its own radio relay systems and their own cable systems that were laid only for military purposes. I don't really know much about that system. They also use telecom cables. Everything that could be used as a regular system or a backup system, they used. They would also resort to one or two parallel systems just in case.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And the civil authorities, for example, the Presidency, the Assembly, the government, did they have a separate communications system apart from what you used in the MUP and what the army used, do you know?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: They used the public system and a little bit of the police system, mostly the telephone lines, for security purposes. Whether we're talking about particular figures whose security is taken care of by the police or because of our people who had a need to communicate with the state organs, this applied in peace time. But the defence ministry or as it was called then the republican secretariat for national defence, had a communications detachment for war time situations which was supposed to be placed at a number of locations in war time with specific personnel and equipment and to secure the communication of those organs with the other structures, that are state structures. But we're only talking about war time requirements in this particular case.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you if you know whether or not the civilian communication network sometimes had connections that were not available to the police. For example, in Pale was the civil communications network able to contact, for example, a Crisis Staff in some municipality for which you didn't have a connection to the MUP system, do you know?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I know this just generally, that a communications centre was set up in Pale, the one that covers the secretariat or the Ministry of Defence, but it didn't have any particular capacities except what it could use through the public telecommunications system. And perhaps it had along some lines the ability to have special connections if they were installed. But I really don't know their plan. I don't know what they had. All I know was that there was that centre. I even dropped by there. It wasn't anything of particular interest that I noticed there. They had the same problem that I did basically, as far as communication was concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know who the head of that centre was at the time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, it was Colonel Milorad Kotlica. Unfortunately he died in the meantime.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And for the civil authorities, do you know who the head of that communications centre was in Pale in 1992? Because I take it Colonel Kotlica was for the military, or am I misunderstanding?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, it was not military. You have to understand, there was an army with its General Staff and it had operational command of the army, and on the other hand there's the Ministry of Defence, which has a completely different function. They don't deal with the raising defences on the territory. They deal with the general defence preparations for the state, in a very broad sense. That detachment was a military detachment and they did wear uniforms when they were in the field, and they did use equipment that could be perhaps qualified, at least some of it, as military equipment because the technical specifications were the same. But they had no direct powers towards the army or the army towards them. They were in contact perhaps with municipalities and some other structures. So I don't know apart from this centre at Pale that there was another communications centre for communication -- for civilian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I see Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, if I may be of assistance, 51, 16, I believe the witness said that detachment was not a military detachment. Maybe you can clarify.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Witness, you heard what Mr. Zecevic said. Can you tell us which is correct. Did that detachment -- was that detachment military or not?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It wasn't military in the sense of being part of the army because they were part of the defence ministry and they were planned for a war time situation and they wore uniforms. When the war start, they put on uniforms, and these are people, for instance, the detachment commander within his section in the Ministry of Defence, was Hasan Redzepagic, a major. I know them all as civilians, but they did have ranks. It was a very specific, peculiar structure, where the hierarchy has to be clearly known, who is in command and who obeys.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Having said that, I guess in your job did you wear uniforms or did you wear civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: You mean before the war or during the war?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Both.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It was up to me. I could wear a uniform or civilian clothes. If I thought I was going to a drill where I wouldn't have to run about the field much, then I went in civilian clothes, but if the weather was inclement and I knew I would get soaked, I would put on a uniform, but I didn't have to.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Too bad you didn't bring your uniform to The Hague. Sorry. I'm disappointed with the weather we've been having. Let me show you next, related to this annual report. Let me show you next 65 ter 068. This is at tab 78. You mentioned that in preparing your part of what went into the annual report, you received information from the CSBs. This document is described as an activity report of communications and cryptographic data protection department for the period of 30 July to 30 September 1992 for the Doboj CSB. Do you recognise the name and signature that's on that document?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. Head of section, Miomir Djekic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. And my English translation has his name spelled as Miomir Cekic with a C with a half banana, but you tell me his correct name is Djekic, which should be --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, right --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The D with a diacritic or sometimes spelled in English as Dj. You knew him as the department chief in Doboj?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. I know him very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And is this the kind of information you would receive from the CSBs to help prepare quarterly and semi-annual and annual reports?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: In general, yes. I just can't see the statistics, for instance, the number of dispatches, I can't see very clearly the text.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I don't see those in this particular text either, but I don't have one for the end of the year.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Because let me tell you, it was not customary for us to do these statistics unless somebody asked for it specifically, for a particular requirement, for a particular occasion. It would be done in the annual report. The statistics were not put in here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'd like to tender that document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1426, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Kezunovic --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Sorry, excuse me, really, I just noticed. I can't see to whom this was sent. It should be in the heading. It just says "report," and I can see in the heading that it's Doboj, and I see the chief of section at the bottom, but I can't be sure that this is a report here addressed to the centre. If it was addressed to the centre, it would say "to the chief." If there was several addressees, they should be named, like communications administration -- unless this is a cover letter saying: Please find attached such and such a report. But this is just about the form. The rest is okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Next I wanted to ask you about where MUP headquarters, the RS MUP, where it was located during 1992. I understand from other evidence in the case that it was not always in the same location. You told us that in April 1992 for a while that you were in Vrace and you were also in Pale. Can you tell us to the best of your knowledge where MUP headquarters were located throughout April through December 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: We among us considered that the base of the MUP is at Pale; however, parts of the MUP were located in different places. Simply, there was no building big enough and with an appropriate layout of premises that we could all sit in one place. The seat of the MUP was at Pale, but we were all stationed in a number of buildings. Some people were in the same place from December to April, others moved several times, like myself. I was briefly at Vrace, then for a while at Lukavica, then I returned to Pale, and then from Kalovita Brda we moved to an installation called Kikinda because it was owned by some business company Kikinda, and that's why they called it that. Others were on Mount Jahorina, but we all thought of it as the location of the MUP with the main location in Pale, but there were several buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was there a time in 1992 where or when the RS MUP headquarters was moved to Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. I personally received orders early in December, official orders, to go to Bijeljina. There was some units, organisational units I mean, that had moved even before me. And at that moment we considered that we had two basic locations of the MUP, one in Pale and one in Bijeljina, that were on a completely equal footing as far as communications were concerned. We would only put in an additional symbol to designate whether something was being sent from Pale or for Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Do you know in -- from April through December 1992 where the minister's office was located. Where was Mr. Stanisic's office during that time-period? And I understand it was not always in the same place?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Again I have to say from the viewpoint of us signals men, the office had two designations: Pale or Bijeljina. The minister could formally be in any of these two locations. We knew where to send him communications, in Pale or in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If you needed or wanted to speak to him personally in Pale, where would you go, what building would you find him in in 1992? And if it's more than one, please tell us about that.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: He would be in one of these two locations, Pale or Bijeljina. I would check with his secretary or his chef de cabinet. I would ask where I could find the minister, if he had time to see me, if he has the possibility, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But in Pale where would you go to find him? Where was his office physically located within Pale, if you know?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: For a while we were at Kalovita Brda, which is a smaller installation, and then we moved into the other building that we called Kikinda. And there was one more building in Pale closer to the centre, between the previous two. And later ministers used that same location. The premises were good and supporting services could be housed next to the minister's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I think it's time for our next break, Mr. Kezunovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. We would resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Just for the record, Your Honours, my colleague co-counsel Krgovic, Dragan, is present at the hearing now. After a big fight, many years.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Kezunovic, I next want to show you a document that's already in evidence, it's Exhibit P160. And I'll tell you, as it's coming up on the screen, it refers to a meeting of MUP officials in Belgrade on the 11th of July, 1992. I see you on the first page as -- listed as one of those attending. Do you recall attending this meeting in Belgrade in July 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I just have two short things to ask you about. One is to clear up a translation issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could look at page 17 of the English and in e-court it's page 17 of the B/C/S as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You're listed as one of those who participated in a discussion. And it says: "Kezunovic on connections" -- top of the page in the English and that fourth paragraph in B/C/S at the very bottom. It says: "Kezunovic (on connections ..." And there's an abbreviation in the B/C/S which has been translated in English as criminal code, but I think it stands for something else. Can you tell us what those two letters are, my Cyrillic's not very good. I think it's --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It's in paragraph 4?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: "Dragan Kezunovic (KZ" --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Cryptographic protection.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Or encoding.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. That makes more sense and I'd just like to note that correction for the record in the English version. And at page -- if we could go to page 28 of the English, I think it's 31 in the B/C/S at the top of both pages. And we're in the section that talks about conclusions that were reached as a result of the meeting, and number 15 is the one I want to ask you about. It says: "Code-names are to be chosen for all SJBs, police stations, centres, and administrations ..." and the responsible party for that is your administration for communications and cryptographic data protection. First of all, can you explain to us what that is, what sorts of code-names were going to be chosen for the SJBs and the centres, et cetera? Is that an actual name? Is it a number? Is it some combination of names and numbers?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think it's the development of a list of names, or rather, number designations for certain organisational units, but I don't know if that's what is meant. If somebody meant the code book, then this is not the most fortunate phrasing. So I cannot really be sure, do I understand the meaning, but I suppose it's the nomenclature. All organisational units should have a number designation that they would put on their dispatches and all the other communications. And these number designations were usually -- that was usually done by the personnel department, not the communications department. But I'm not saying it's absolutely impossible that we did it. In any case, I didn't do this. This had to be developed for the ministry to operate.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was there already some kind of designator system in place as of July 1992, maybe a carry-over from the previous MUP, do you know?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It could not be fully carried over, but there was a certain analogy and the same logic, according to which we designated our communications centres and our outside stations. It was not the purpose to make it similar to the previous system, but it was certainly easier and more identifiable to people. For instance, my unit had the designation 4 or 5, I can't remember exactly, but it was the same as before the war. For instance, the uniformed police was line 1, the crime investigation department was 2, et cetera. Anyway, it reflected the organisation as it developed and spread.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me ask you a little further to be sure I understand this. You talked about the lines of work or the administrations within the organisation. 01 is uniformed police, and I think 02 is crime prevention, and communications was 04. And as I understand it, the organisation in which you worked would also have a designator. So MUP at the seat, at the head, MUP headquarters would have some sort of designator, and you as an individual, would you have a designator as well?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Not in this sense, that I would have my own number. I was chief of administration, the administration comprised certain sections with heads of sections. In some administrations they were sectors, with chief of sectors -- however, there was another thing. If phone book, so to call it, was made for the users of ultra short-wave communications, not -- which is not the same as short-wave communications, then all the participants that would appear in that book had their own code-name, calling name. That is something entirely different. It was not the same as the number. You knew what code-name the MUP in the headquarters had, you knew the code-names were for centres. It would be usually a code-name with two components, one name of a geographical feature plus a number. But that was the case with the republic SUP before.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And there you're talking about short-wave radio communications?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: These are ultra short-wave communications. Those are the radios carried by policemen in the field or in their vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And as I understand it, that would be, for example, a small police platoon or something might have a designator of, pick a name, cobra, and the commander would be Cobra 1; am I understanding correctly?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that's the same principle.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, with regard to the MUP headquarters and the CSB and the SJB, they could have a nomenclature of where there would be a number for the CSB or the SJB, and within that there would be a subnumber for the various administrations. For example, Zvornik -- let's just pick a number and say it would be 150, and 150-04 would mean the source was from communications in Zvornik police station. Am I understanding correctly?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Generally speaking, yes. If a line of work at the headquarters of the ministry has a certain number, that number extends down to the last organisational units in the municipality, through the centre, the regional unit, down to the lowest-level one. And you would know that a communications group in the same line of work would have the same number as the corresponding administration at the MUP headquarters, plus there would be another symbol to designate the unit in question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Where are we going with these technicalities?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, it may be useful in examining individual documents that were sent. Sometimes to be able to identify based on the number where it came from, if there's no indication otherwise. We may have some documents where it doesn't say "Zvornik police station." It may say -- it may say a number, and that can help us identify the sender or the receiver or the person mentioned to do something or respond to something. I'll stop there and move on to tab number 66, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And we can just look at the first page. This is an order from Minister Stanisic on the 23rd of July, 1992. I'm sorry, this is Exhibit 1D058. And, Mr. Kezunovic, I'm interested in the introductory paragraph for this order. It says: "Proceeding from conclusions reached at the meeting of executive employees held on 11 July 1992," which seems to refer to the meeting in Belgrade that you attended, "the meeting of the collegiate body held on 23 July 1992 ..." Let me ask you, first of all: What does that term "collegiate body" mean in this context? Can you tell us who the members of the MUP collegium or collegiate body were on July 23rd, 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The minister, the deputy minister, the heads of the section, assistant ministers, I'm not sure whether it was also the commander of the special brigade or the detachment, as the unit was called at the time. Also -- but in any case, this was something that was regulated on the rules of internal operation, where it is stated who comprises the collegium, the broader collegium, and also if necessary other persons could be invited to attend if there was a need. In any case, the leadership along all the professional lines of work, of course the deputies, the heads of the departments, and maybe some other leadership officials, and I think probably in the rules on internal organisation they are stated. I don't need to mention each such case myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. In your answer you just made reference to the broader collegium. I might use the term extended collegium. How was that different from the regular collegium? What additional persons would make up the broader collegium, if you know?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Usually the chiefs of the centres of public security. Perhaps in the beginning also the chiefs of the state security centres; and if needed, somebody else too.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. In 1992, between April and the end of December, how frequently were there meetings of the collegium with the heads of the administration?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Between April and - I'm sorry, which period?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the end of the year. Did you meet once a month? Once a week? How often, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I cannot remember, but I assume that it was at least once a month.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How about meetings of the extended collegium, do you recall how often that group met in 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I really cannot say with any certainty. I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Would it be less often than the regular collegium?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, yes. In any case, yes, it would be less often.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. That makes sense to me. At any of the collegium meetings you attended in 1992, do you remember the subject of paramilitary groups being discussed?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I do, but really in the most general terms. I cannot tell you when this was, which session, who was discussed, but I know that the minister did respond strongly and asked the police and the leadership to deal with these matters and to clear that up.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you remember being interviewed by representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor in 2004?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you recall in that meeting mentioning two different paramilitary groups that you recalled being talked about in collegium meetings?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I recall - and again I have to stress only in general terms, and I don't know the name of the group or who was at the head of the group, who commanded the group - somewhere along the road to Zvornik, and I know that they stopped me as well. I wasn't mistreated in any particular way, but for example, they kept me for an hour or so. I couldn't continue on my way. I don't know the name of the group, but I do know that these things happened. I couldn't say exactly what the date was. Perhaps I can recall what period it was, but I really cannot remember the date. This is something that happened two or three times when I was going down that road towards Bijeljina, and that's what happened to me. The group was later arrested and eliminated. They were dealt with and then the road later was clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you recall what was being said about that group in the collegium meeting?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't remember what was said specifically, but I do remember that the minister was angry and that he reacted firmly and that he demanded that these people be dealt with, the matter be dealt with. And I know that he even criticised somebody from the police who was in charge of that, shouted at them, and said, "If you're not capable of doing that, just say so and we'll assign someone else to do it." I don't remember the specifics of this, however.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was your memory about the events in Zvornik when you were stopped and about discussions at the collegium, was your memory about those things better in 2004 when you were interviewed than it is as you sit here today?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Possibly it was, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I want to read you something and ask if it refreshes your recollection. At page 46 of your interview --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, isn't the practice to have the witness read it himself and then ask the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'm afraid I don't have it in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Because the -- I don't suppose I need to remind you that a refreshing-memory document is not part of the -- is not evidential, and if you were to read it, you would be in effect making it part of the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. Let me pass on that for now and perhaps I'll have B/C/S in the morning during my last portion. I'll do it that way. I understand your concern.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In terms of when you were stopped at this location, do you remember if it was before or after the meeting in Belgrade on July 11th?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't remember. I can't remember now. I know that I passed there two or three times. In any case, it was before or around that date. Most probably before because this road goes from Pale via Sokolac, Han Pijesak, Vlasenica. It doesn't go directly to Zvornik. You would go through Sekovici via a detour, but then it comes back to the part of the road that leads from Zvornik to Kalesija towards Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Next I'd like to show you a document that is 65 ter number 2747. This is at tab 24. Now, Mr. Kezunovic, this is dated the 26 of April, 1992, and it appears to be from the ministry in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could scroll all the way to the top of the B/C/S page. There is a fax header on the B/C/S copy that has not been reflected on the English translation. Do you see that, Mr. Kezunovic, where it says in English "from" and then "Srpska Republika BiH MUP." And then if we could shrink it a little bit so we can see the phone number as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I take it this document was -- oh, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm really sorry. Your Honours, if the intention of my learned friend is to suggest that this document was sent in 1992 over the fax, I believe this is not adequate because the date from the fax message is clearly missing -- at least on my copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, that goes to weight, I guess. I'll ask this witness if they had fax machines capable of sending messages on the 26th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sorry, you said the date appears in the header of --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, I don't have a date on the header.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, mustn't we take the document as it is and at the end of the day make what we can of it? It is --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I understand. I think this is already in evidence as P1420.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, yes. But in terms of the -- I think it can be said it's notorious that the headers of faxes are not necessarily accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So there's room for argument, but as I said, we take the document as it is and --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, I have some questions that may bear on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Kezunovic, can you explain why this document would have English on it, the words "from" and "phone no."?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, this is simply made by the fax software, so that the company or an individual using the fax can put in their name so that the person or entity receiving a message from that fax has confirmation that it comes from that company or individual. But that doesn't necessarily have to mean that. I can get that and put it somewhere else, even though if I didn't change the name of the company or the person that is sending it. This "from" part, it doesn't necessarily have to be accurate, the phone number either. I mean, you could take that as being accurate or not. It doesn't have to be. Usually there is a confirmation report that is printed, whether the message was transferred or delivered successfully or not from/to, and this would contain the accurate information. But here we don't have that confirmation as an attachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, can you remember now whether or not you had fax machines in the RS MUP that were being used in late April 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: We did, but I have to say that as per the custom that was inherited and our position towards faxes as means of communication, this was a means for open communication, and the intention was not to send any confidential information via fax. It was procured before the war so that some services, like the financial services, administration that worked with companies procuring equipment and material, could communicate more easily. This means of communication, fax communication, was intended only for such cases, for open communication. It was just a means of communication. You could easily take information from faxes parallel information could be taken at the same time. So it was not considered to be a secure means of communication. We did not use it in the communication centres for confidential information or information that was supposed to be encrypted.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: A question about the addressees. You see the five security services centres listed here along with the names of the heads of those services. Is that information correct based on your knowledge of who was in those positions in April 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It's correct. The information there is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you about Mr. Jesuric and the head in Bijeljina. Do you know what other positions he held in the MUP later in 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I know that he was the chief of the Bijeljina station. I know that he was the chief of the department for aliens I think at one point in time. I don't know the full name. Perhaps he was the chief of one of the administrations even later. I cannot remember the chronology of the posts that he was appointed to.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know what he was by profession before 1992? Was he a policeman?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think that he's a lawyer by profession.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: A lawyer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You mentioned that certain kinds of documents shouldn't be sent by fax because of the confidential nature of their content. Did you have a chance to look at the content of this one during proofing? It talks about the minister transferring his authority to the CSB heads regarding distribution of certain employees.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: This dispatch was sent to the chiefs of the centres. Do you mean what was the intention with this dispatch?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No. Let me try and rephrase my question. This doesn't seem to be information about -- of an operational nature. It seemed to be more administrative in terms of delegating to the heads of centres the authority to choose employees for certain positions within the centres. And my question is: In your opinion in your job, would this be something that would necessarily have to be sent as a coded message ?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I have to repeat one thing. I never worked on sending out dispatches. This was done by operators at the communications centre who receive a dispatch, log it in, and then encrypt it, if necessary note down the manner of its transmission, and do all the actions that have to be taken in relation to that dispatch. They didn't remember the contents of the dispatch themselves either. They would just read it because if they needed to type it out, they would do it, and then they would forget it because new ones were coming in. Nobody remembered the contents. Myself in particular, I wasn't really looking at who was sending what to whom. I didn't need to do that. It wasn't in the description of my duties unless the addressee in the dispatch was myself, and then if it was I would act in accordance with what was stated in the dispatch. If you're asking for my personal opinion in terms of this dispatch, since this was at the beginning, this is the 20th of April, if I'm not mistaken, 1992, you can't really see it very well here, you're right that this is an administrative procedural question up to a point. The appointment of personnel. Before the war there was a procedure which was a bit more complex, more complicated in terms of electing or choosing an employee according to all the criteria that they were supposed to fulfill. And also, before the war the republican SUP would have to approve each of the appointment, the relevant, professional section. If the Prijedor centre had to appoint a communications operative, we would have to approve that, look at all the material the centre had prepared that had to do with the employment of that particular worker. We would also have to review. Probably the intention of this was to speed up the procedure. In this period there was no time to go through that whole process. Simply, the centre chiefs were authorised to organise that matter, again in keeping with all the set criteria and procedures. I assume that that was the point, the intention.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you about fax machines.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can we look at Exhibit P546. This is located at tab 14.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This is to all CSBs. The chief from the minister dated 20 April 1992. It says: "I hereby order that fax machines be obtained and installed in all security services centres and all public security stations ..." I think you told us during proofing that there was a shortage of fax machines available to you at that time, in April 1992; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, I'm not unmindful of the answer that you gave to a question put to you by Judge Harhoff near the beginning of the current session, but is this really necessary?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I had a suggestion that one document that had a fax header, Your Honour, was not faxed in 1992. So I think I need to establish that there were fax machines being used by the MUP in April 1992. Unless the Defence is willing to agree that's true, I think I have to prove it. And this question is leading to some questions about a different fax header we'll see on another document that may explain something that on its face appears unusual.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Kezunovic, was there a shortage of fax machines available for the RS MUP in April 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Do you mean MUP at the seat or generally all the organisational units in the MUP including the ones in the field?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I mean both, headquarters and in the field.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: They weren't all covered with that equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in some cases when MUP wasn't able to find them within their own warehouses or able to purchase them from outside, did they sometimes borrow them or requisition them from private enterprises or commercial enterprises?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Possibly this happened. I personally didn't borrow one or requisition one from anyone for my own needs. Perhaps some did do that in the field. A lot of that - and I can't really put it in the chronological order - but a lot of equipment was received in various ways, through donations and, I don't know, from people who live and work abroad. But this happened later. They would do that based on what they felt would be the most useful thing. I don't believe that they particularly discussed with anyone else what was required or what was a priority. But again, I repeat, the fax is a open communications means, and if we do have telephone communications that would mean that automatically we would have fax communication available too. But there are also these other circumstances, meaning that it was vulnerable to listening in or taking information from it. So that would be a factor in the final decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me show you another document. This is P543. It's at tab 10. This is a document to the CSB centres from the minister, and you'll see a fax header on this one with a date and time, 18 April 1992. I can't read that word or pronounce it in the upper left, "buducnost." Can you tell us what that was?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: There's something else before that word, an acronym, that I can't make out. It must have been a company or an institution. There's something before "buducnost" where the cursor is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know what -- sorry. Do you know what "buducnost" was?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like next to show you an exhibit at tab 50. This is 65 ter number 0153. It's a payroll document apparently for the month of May 1992. And I'd like to show you the second page in both English and B/C/S. The last group appears to be --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm sorry, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This is exactly the document which I withdraw this morning. It's also P867, it's the identical document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Ah. Well, no, actually as far as I can tell there is a difference. What I have is P867 is the same document but without signatures in my B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, that is correct. I'm sorry, that is correct --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It does appear to be the same type --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It does appear the same document except for the signatures, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So what I'd like to do is substitute this one with the signatures as the B/C/S version, if I can do that with my case manager and the Legal Officer, once I've had the defendant (sic) confirm something about the signatures.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Kezunovic, you recognise your name on the list?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I can find it, but I didn't get an answer as to the accused or the witness recognising their name.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't understand that. Mr. Kezunovic, you see your name on the page there as number 1 under the last group of names?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And is that your signature on the right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. The other 11 individuals in that group, were they the people who worked in your administration in May of 1992, Mr. Andric and the others?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. I don't know the best way mechanically to do it, whether we substitute it or we cross-reference it, but I would like this to be one that goes into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The Registry will deal with the technical details --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: -- of how it's done. But the Chamber agrees.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Next I would like to show you -- I have a few payroll documents that I want to show you for various purposes. The next is -- it's at tab 72, it's 65 ter number 3128, and it appears to be for the month of July 1992. You see number 2 shows Slobodan Skipina as the under-secretary and number 7 Vlastimir Kusmuk as an assistant to the minister. And to your knowledge is that the positions that those two men held in July 1992 in the MUP?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And I see you're number 5 on the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we tender 65 ter 3128?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Is this disputed at all? I mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, sometimes I think it's important to corroborate -- I don't know if it's disputed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, it's not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Sorry? You should --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, it is not disputed that these persons were the -- were at the seat of the MUP at this particular time in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Is it also not disputed that they later were shifted to the position of advisors to the minister, both Mr. Skipina and Mr. Kusmuk?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I don't think that that is also disputed. We had the documents on -- I'm not sure about Mr. Kusmuk at this point, but for Mr. Skipina Slobodan, I'm 100 per cent sure that I know the decision of the minister to appoint him as the advisor. And Mr. Dragan Kijac took over his position as the chief of national -- under-secretary for national security, somewhere in August 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And while you're in a good mood, is it also not disputed that their salaries as advisors were reduced, they were less than the salaries they had as an assistant minister or the --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you're definitely pushing me too far. I can't tell you about the salaries, but I don't -- if you give me time, I might not be disputing that as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, that's why I'm trying to show the documents, because I'll show another document what their salary was when they were in those new positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I don't see -- I mean -- I don't see the relevance of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, we -- I don't know if -- I guess I can say this in front of the witness. It's the Prosecution's position that those two particular individuals were placed in high positions at the beginning. They were later, we say, sidelined when they were shifted to the advisor position without any real tasks to do, and that there was a reason for that. And the reasons for that relate to different philosophies between the accused and those gentlemen. It may go --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But hold on --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: -- maybe at this point the witness should take off his earphones. Mr. Kezunovic, would you be good enough to take off your earphones?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, he understands quite a bit of English. That's all I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I mean, if you want to put questions to Mr. Kezunovic directly on the reasons why these two gentlemen were sidelined, as you say, then, you know, just put those questions and get directly to it because the Chamber is wary of the amount of documents that is being introduced into evidence for reasons that are not quite clear. And we have seen already twice today documents which have been duplicated inadvertently. So let's direct the questions to the witnesses that will enable you and the Defence to elicit the information which is relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If I may just briefly comment, Your Honours. Mr. Skipina was the witness here in this case, so we have his testimony in this case. And I cannot remember on top of my head, but I'm sure that he was asked this question. Vlastimir Kusmuk is the one that's on the list, but apparently our friends from the Prosecution want to withdraw him. Now, if that is an issue of the -- that the OTP wants to rely on or thinks it's an important issue in this case, well then both of these gentlemen should have been asked that question, the ones which were appointed as the advisors to the minister and before holding the position of the assistant minister. I'm not saying that this question -- this question cannot be put to the -- to this witness as well, but it would be only expected that the actual persons are called to testify to this facts. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I can have an agreement from the Defence that these payroll documents are authentic, well that's all I want to do is get the documents in. I can make my argument later at the relevant time, at the end of the case, if I need be I have the information from which I can argue that there is a logical inference to be drawn from timing and changes in pay and moves tied in with other evidence. I don't need to ask this witness and I don't know if I can't have the Defence tell me that they're not going to object to my tendering these documents, then I need to show them to a witness who has knowledge about them, unless I can satisfy Your Honours that I can get these in through a bar table motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yeah, I was going to say I thought it was an either/or. Either lead the evidence directly or seek to tender the documents. If the evidence could be had through the direct testimony of a witness, that would be it, that would be as much as you would need.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. But covering the point that was made about whether this duplication and the Chamber's concerned about a lot of documents -- I need a lot of documents sometimes to make the argument. And the fact that one witness, for example, Mr. Skipina was here and testified about something, sometimes Your Honours may not find it sufficient to rely on the word of one witness about one event if there is a document that supports it or opposes it. That's something you will factor in through your total consideration about the credibility of a witness about that point. So that's why I'm trying to get in some of these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The practical concern that the Chamber has is that apart from at the end of the exercise unnecessarily burdening some landfill somewhere, is that you having telegraphed the purpose for which you wished to tender these documents, it is an argument which when you come to make it we -- and I'm trying to phrase this correctly so that I'm not suggesting that we have reached a conclusion, but it seems that we would have some difficulty accepting because the documents by themselves wouldn't -- without more it seems to us, support the conclusion which you are inviting the Chamber to draw inexorably merely from what the documents contain and therein lies our problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honours, and I'm hoping that the documents won't be the only thing I have to make the argument by the time we get to the end of the Prosecution case, that there are or is at least one witnesses to come that will speak to some of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: By majority we are going to get on with it and allow the documents to be admitted, Judge Harhoff dissenting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. So save time I will skip over some of the additional ones now and talk with my learned friends across the way about the possibility of maybe introducing the others through the bar table without having to ask the witness it that's his name.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document will become Exhibit P1427, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Kezunovic, how did you know Mr. Stanisic? When and where did you first meet him?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: You mean when I first met him? Before the war, when he was working in the city secretariat for internal affairs, Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And Mr. Zupljanin, how and when did you first meet him?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Also before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Earlier I asked you about where the MUP headquarters were located and where the minister's office was in 1992. Did you have occasion where you had difficulty in locating the minister when someone from the government was trying to find him?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I told you that the MUP was housed in several locations in Pale. The president of the republic and the government were also housed in a number of buildings, and we didn't meet every day for practical reasons. It was neither necessary nor possible to meet every day. Everyone dealt with their responsibilities the best they could, the best that could be organised. Plus, he wasn't necessarily always there when I needed him. I first had to locate him and then see if it was possible to meet. It was mostly a technical matter. We were not all in the same building in the same place.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you ever have a conversation one-on-one with Mico Stanisic about your difficulty in locating him when you needed him sometimes?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think once at the request of operators, signals men, but that was early in April, at the very beginning when we were at Kalovita Brda. They kind of delegated me -- not really delegated me because they couldn't give me an assignment, but they asked me nicely because somebody from the government was looking for the minister and they didn't know how to find him because at that time the service was not as established and as well equipped as before the war when we had duty service and all the communications equipment was fully in place and in operation and we were all stationed in the same building, all the various organisational units in the same place. And of course if the minister was on a field mission, moving around the duty service or his own chef de cabinet or his technical secretary or somebody would have to keep track of all the senior officials, not only that minister but all the other senior executives because, for instance, it might have become necessary to convene a meeting of the collegium. And the person who would get that task, be it from the office of the minister or from the communications centre, that person would have to know who is where so as to deal with it operationally. In that sense, the minister would have to be on the radar, I mean assistants also but assistants, of course, are not as important as the minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. I understand that at MUP headquarters there would be 24 hours a day somebody who was on duty, as I think the term was "operations officer." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: In principle, yes. But conditionally speaking, at the beginning - and this is why - there would be one or two people who would be on a 24-hour shift. If that person was alone, he would also have a bed there and he wouldn't be able to leave the room except to go to the toilet. So if we're talking about this initial period which was relatively short, that's how it was. Later on the service was better organised, it had more personnel, more decent premises to accommodate these people on such jobs.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: On this occasion when some of your colleagues asked you to try and locate the minister, did you try and find him through the duty officer?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Nobody tasked me as me to look for him. The normal thing to do was to call the duty service or the communications centre and ask where he was, and that signals man would inform me and ask me -- not that same moment, but when he ran into me. In fact, he would be just answering my question: How is it going? Are you having any problems? And they would share with me their difficulties and they would mention that as well. It's not only about this minister, but a minister, any minister, from the cabinet would call the duty operator at the MUP or the signals man but even not directly but through his secretary.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Kezunovic, let me ask you, as a result of that inability to locate the minister on that occasion, did you personally have a conversation with Mico Stanisic about that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, yes, once. I mentioned that as well because other people mentioned it to me, and among 15 or 20 other questions and issues that had to be dealt with, I mentioned to him that as well. It was not only my problem; it was a general issue. If you were looking for anyone else, it was the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand. What was his response to you when you raised it with him?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KEZUNOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I can't remember it word for word, but among other things he said that even those who are insisting on it should not insist too much. Because moving around on the ground at that time was an issue of personal security and safety, among other things. There was not a single section of any road leading from Pale in any direction that was completely safe from nasty surprises, and it was also for that reason that he was perhaps reluctant to share his travel plans, and I suppose it was the same with the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think we've reached the point to break for the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Kezunovic, I must remind you that you, having been sworn as a witness and your testimony not being complete, that you cannot have any communication with counsel from either side, and in such conversations as you may have outside the chamber you cannot discuss your testimony. So we take the adjournment now to resume in Courtroom I tomorrow morning at 9.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 11th day of June, 2010, at 9.00 a.m.
